summary: Documents an extended key usage (EKU) X.509 extension that restricts a certificate to use with a SIP service. It gives rules for SIP implementations and guidance for certificate issuers. It is an Experimental protocol, not a standard.

eli5.summary: A sticker on a key that says it only opens the phone-service door and no others.

how do sip proxies verify certificates
subtitle: A certificate extension that restricts a domain name to use only for SIP.

tldr.problem: A DNS name like example.com often serves multiple purposes: SIP service, email, web service. Certificate authorities issued certificates binding that name to the domain, but a SIP server could not tell if a certificate was for SIP use or for something else.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines an Extended Key Usage (EKU) X.509 certificate extension called id-kp-sipDomain that marks a certificate as valid only for SIP services.
tldr.outcome: SIP implementations can now check this extension to confirm that a peer's certificate is authorized specifically for SIP, preventing misuse of general-purpose certificates.

today: RFC 5924 is Experimental. It defines the id-kp-sipDomain EKU extension for restricting X.509 certificates to SIP use only.

sections.title: The Problem of Shared Domain Names
sections.content:
The Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) uses X.509 certificates to authenticate proxy servers. When two proxies connect, they exchange certificates to prove they control a SIP domain. A domain name like example.com is unique across the Internet, but it is often used for multiple services: SIP for voice, SMTP for mail, HTTPS for websites. A Certificate Authority may issue one certificate for example.com that covers all these uses.

The problem arises because a SIP proxy that receives such a multi-purpose certificate has no way to know that the certificate is authorized for SIP. The certificate might be valid for web service only, and the sender might not be authorized as a SIP domain. Without additional information, the proxy cannot safely trust the certificate.
sections.eli5: Imagine a key that opens both your house and your office. If you give someone the key, they can enter either place. A sticker that says the key only opens the office door would make it safer.

sections.title: The Extended Key Usage Extension
sections.content:
X.509 certificates already support an Extended Key Usage (EKU) extension that limits what a certificate can be used for. For example, an EKU might say a certificate is valid only for authenticating TLS servers, not for code signing. This RFC defines a new EKU value called id-kp-sipDomain with the object identifier {id-kp 20}. When a certificate includes this EKU, it asserts that the certificate is valid only for SIP domain authentication.

The EKU extension in a certificate contains a list of purposes. An application can require that a specific purpose be present before accepting the certificate. This RFC recommends that a Certificate Authority issuing a certificate meant solely for SIP domain binding MUST include the id-kp-sipDomain value in the EKU extension.
sections.eli5: The EKU is a label in the certificate that says what you can use it for. This RFC adds a new label that says it is only for SIP.

sections.title: How SIP Implementations Use the EKU
sections.content: When a SIP implementation receives a certificate, it MUST examine the Extended Key Usage values to determine if the certificate is acceptable for SIP use. The validation rules are as follows. If the certificate does not contain any EKU extension, it is a matter of local policy whether to accept it, but accepting it is more interoperable since many existing certificates have no EKU. If the certificate contains the id-kp-sipDomain EKU value, the implementation MUST accept it as valid for SIP. If the certificate contains the id-kp-anyExtendedKeyUsage value, acceptance is a matter of local policy. If the EKU extension exists but does not contain id-kp-sipDomain or the anyExtendedKeyUsage value, the certificate MUST NOT be accepted for SIP.
sections.eli5: When you get a certificate for SIP, you check the label. If it says SIP, you use it. If the label says something else, you do not. If there is no label, you can decide based on your own rules.

sections.title: Certificate Authority Responsibilities
sections.content: Certificate Authorities that issue SIP domain certificates must ensure that they insert the correct EKU extension in the certificate. For a certificate that binds a domain name only to a SIP service and not to any other service, the Certificate Authority MUST include the id-kp-sipDomain EKU extension. The procedures and practices of the CA must ensure that the correct values for the EKU extension and the subjectAltName are inserted in each certificate issued. This prevents accidental issuance of multi-purpose certificates when a SIP-only certificate was requested.
sections.eli5: When a Certificate Authority issues a certificate, it must put the right label on it. If the customer asks for SIP only, it must not label it as general-purpose.
